section.title: Beelzebul and the Sign of Jonah
section.sectionRationale: The conflict reaches its crisis. Faced with an undeniable exorcism, the Pharisees credit it to Satan, and Jesus exposes the absurdity and danger of their charge, warning of the unforgivable blasphemy against the Spirit. He teaches that words reveal the heart, refuses their demand for a sign except the sign of Jonah, His resurrection, and redefines His true family as those who do the Father's will.
section.thesis: By the Spirit of God Jesus overthrows Satan's kingdom, binding the strong man, so that to credit His work to the devil is a hardened blasphemy that reveals the heart; He gives no sign but His death and resurrection, warns against empty reform, and gathers a new family of all who do the Father's will.
section.frameNote: Six beats: the charge of Beelzebul answered; the blasphemy against the Spirit; words revealing the heart; the sign of Jonah; the return of the unclean spirit; and the true family of Jesus.

verses.text: Then a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to Jesus, and He healed the man so that he could speak and see.
The crowds were astounded and asked, “Could this be the Son of David?”
But when the Pharisees heard this, they said, “Only by {{beelzeboul|Beelzebul}}, the prince of demons, does this man drive out demons.”
Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand.
If Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then can his kingdom stand?
And if I drive out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? So then, they will be your judges.
But if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
Or again, how can anyone enter a strong man’s house and steal his possessions, unless he first ties up the strong man? Then he can plunder his house.
He who is not with Me is against Me, and he who does not gather with Me scatters.
Therefore I tell you, every sin and {{blasphemia|blasphemy}} will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.
Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the one to come.

units.label: Words reveal the heart
units.note: out of the overflow of the heart

verses.text: Make a tree good and its fruit will be good, or make a tree bad and its fruit will be bad, for a tree is known by its fruit.
You brood of vipers, how can you who are evil say anything good? For out of the overflow of the {{kardia|heart}} the mouth speaks.
The good man brings good things out of his good store of treasure, and the evil man brings evil things out of his evil store of treasure.
But I tell you that men will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word they have spoken.
For by your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned.”

units.label: The sign of Jonah
units.note: three days in the heart of the earth

verses.text: Then some of the scribes and Pharisees said to Him, “Teacher, we want to see a {{semeion|sign}} from You.”
Jesus replied, “A wicked and adulterous generation demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.
For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
The men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and now One greater than Jonah is here.
The Queen of the South will rise at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and now One greater than Solomon is here.
When an unclean spirit comes out of a man, it passes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it.
Then it says, ‘I will return to the house I left.’ On its return, it finds the house vacant, swept clean, and put in order.

Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they go in and dwell there. And the final plight of that man is worse than the first. So will it be with this wicked generation.”

units.label: The true family
units.note: whoever does the will of My Father

verses.text: While Jesus was still speaking to the crowds, His mother and brothers stood outside, wanting to speak to Him.
Someone told Him, “Look, Your mother and brothers are standing outside, wanting to speak to You.”
But Jesus replied, “Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?”
Pointing to His disciples, He said, “Here are My mother and My brothers.
For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.”

beelzeboul.gloss: Beelzebul, a name for the prince of demons, that is, Satan. The Pharisees use it to explain away Jesus' exorcism, crediting the Spirit's work to the devil, the very charge Jesus warns is unforgivable when it hardens into settled rejection.

blasphemia.gloss: Blasphemy, slander, defiant speech against God. Every blasphemy can be forgiven except the blasphemy against the Spirit, the deliberate, hardened calling of God's evident work the devil's, which shows a heart closed against the only One who brings repentance.

kardia.gloss: Heart, the inner core of thought, will, and affection. Words are not incidental; out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks, so speech is a reliable index of the heart, by which one is finally acquitted or condemned.

semeion.gloss: Sign, a miraculous token meant to authenticate. The leaders demand a sign despite all they have seen; Jesus refuses any but the sign of Jonah, His three days in the earth and resurrection, the decisive proof of His identity.

basic.context: Jesus frees a blind and mute demoniac, and the crowds wonder if He is the Messiah. The Pharisees, unable to deny the miracle, claim He casts out demons by Satan. Jesus shows how absurd that is, a kingdom cannot war against itself, and reveals that He acts by the Spirit of God, having bound the strong man. He warns of the unforgivable blasphemy against the Spirit, teaches that words reveal the heart, refuses a sign except His resurrection, and names His true family as those who do God's will.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as the turning point where opposition curdles into blasphemy. Jesus' logic about the divided kingdom and the strong man interprets His exorcisms as the invasion of Satan's realm by God's reign. The warning about blaspheming the Spirit must be read in context: it is the hardened, deliberate rejection the Pharisees model, not an accidental word. The sign of Jonah points ahead to the cross and resurrection.
basic.originalLanguages: The Pharisees credit Jesus' power to Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Jesus warns of blasphemy against the Spirit, a defiant rejection that cannot be forgiven while it stands. He teaches that words flow from the heart, the inner self, and so reveal it. And He refuses their demand for a sign, giving only the sign of Jonah, His death and resurrection.
basic.typology: Jonah's three days in the fish foreshadow Jesus' three days in the tomb and His rising. The men of Nineveh who repented and the Queen of the South who sought Solomon's wisdom foreshadow the outsiders who respond while the privileged reject. And binding the strong man fulfills the promised overthrow of the powers of darkness by God's reign.
basic.christ: Jesus is the stronger one who binds Satan and plunders his house, the bringer of God's kingdom by the Spirit. He is greater than Jonah and greater than Solomon, prophet and king in one. And the sign He gives is His own resurrection, the heart of the gospel, by which He is vindicated as the Son of Man.
basic.god: God's kingdom is advancing by His Spirit, overthrowing the reign of evil in the ministry of Jesus. God will hold people accountable for their words, which reveal their hearts. And He is forming a new family defined not by blood but by doing His will, gathered around His Son.
basic.crossReferences: Jonah 1 and 2 give the three days in the fish. 1 Kings 10 tells of the Queen of Sheba seeking Solomon. Isaiah 49 speaks of dividing the spoil of the strong. And Hebrews 6 warns against a hardened falling away that cannot be renewed to repentance.
basic.oneStory: At the crisis of the conflict, Jesus reveals that His exorcisms are the in-breaking of God's kingdom, binding the strong man. To call this the devil's work is a hardening blasphemy that seals the heart. Jesus gives no sign but His resurrection, warns that outsiders who repent will condemn the privileged who reject Him, and gathers a new family of all who do the Father's will, the family the whole story has been forming.

context.literary:
Chapter 12 is built as a ladder of escalating conflict, and this section is its top rung. The chapter opens with two Sabbath disputes, verses 1 to 14, and then pauses on a long quotation from Isaiah 42, verses 18 to 21, in which God's chosen Servant has His Spirit put upon Him and will not quarrel or cry out. Matthew sets that portrait deliberately before the Beelzebul charge. The Pharisees have just plotted to destroy Jesus, verse 14, and now they are about to attribute to Satan the very Spirit that Isaiah said God would place on His Servant.

The unit then runs as a series of answers to two kinds of speech. In verses 22 to 37 the question is what Jesus' words and works are, and what the Pharisees' words reveal about them. In verses 38 to 45 the demand for a sign is met with a refusal and three images: Jonah, the Queen of the South, and the returning spirit. Verses 46 to 50 close the chapter with a scene that looks like an interruption but is in fact its conclusion.

Notice the repeated comparisons with a rising scale. In verse 6 Jesus has already said that something greater than the temple is here; now He says something greater than Jonah, verse 41, and greater than Solomon, verse 42. The prophet, the king and the sanctuary were the three great institutions of Israel's religion, and Jesus stands above each. The tree and fruit sayings of verses 33 to 35 also echo the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 7:16 to 20, tying the controversy back to the ethics of the kingdom.

Finally, the section is a hinge. The conflict has no resolution here. It simply gives way, in chapter 13, to parables spoken to the same crowds, and the family scene that ends chapter 12 sets up the new household of listeners who are gathered in chapter 13.
context.historical:
Exorcism was not unknown in Jewish Galilee. Jesus' question in verse 27, 'by whom do your sons drive them out?', assumes that the Pharisees' own circle practised it and would not call their own successes satanic. Josephus tells of exorcisms credited to the tradition of Solomon, which explains why Jesus later sets Himself alongside Solomon, verse 42. What was new was not the casting out of demons but the authority with which Jesus did it: He does not invoke a name, perform a ritual or use a formula, and He does it in the open for the benefit of the afflicted.

The charge of verse 24 was a clever one, because it could not deny the miracle. In a world where wonders were believed from every side, the only way to discredit a wonder was to question its source. Beelzebul was probably a variant of the name of the Philistine god Baal-zebub of Ekron, whom King Ahaziah consulted in 2 Kings 1:2; the form 'Baal-zebul' is generally taken to mean something like 'lord of the house', which may be why Jesus can speak of the head of the house being called Beelzebul in Matthew 10:25 and then of a strong man's house here. The people of Galilee would have heard the name as a mocking nickname for the chief of the unclean spirits.

The demand for a sign came from scribes and Pharisees, the teachers of the Law, who knew from Deuteronomy 13:1 to 5 and 18:20 to 22 that prophets were tested by their message and their fruit. They had already seen Jesus heal, cleanse and exorcise. Asking for yet another proof was not research but delay.

The comparison to Nineveh and Sheba would have stung in a Jewish audience. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that had destroyed the northern kingdom, and was remembered for its brutality. Sheba, usually placed in the southwest of Arabia, lay at the far edge of the known world. Both were Gentile, and Jesus says they will rise at the judgment to testify against the covenant people.
context.canonical:
The chapter's central controversy takes up the older confession of the magicians in Egypt. Faced with the plague of gnats they said to Pharaoh, 'This is the finger of God,' Exodus 8:19, and then Pharaoh hardened his heart. Luke's account of the same saying has Jesus say 'by the finger of God,' Luke 11:20, so that Matthew's 'Spirit of God' and Luke's phrase explain each other. What Egypt's magicians admitted, the Pharisees will not.

The image of the strong man in verse 29 draws on Isaiah 49:24 to 25, where the captives of the mighty are taken away and the LORD Himself contends with the one who contends with Zion, and on Isaiah 53:12, where the Servant divides the spoils with the strong. The Servant of Isaiah 42, quoted in Matthew 12:18 to 21, is the same figure, so the chapter ties the Servant's anointing, His conflict and His victory together.

The sign of Jonah appears twice in Matthew, here and in Matthew 16:4, and Luke gives it in 11:29 to 32. John's Gospel carries the same theme in the temple saying of John 2:18 to 22, where the sign asked for is again answered by Jesus' death and rising. Paul fixes the third day in the earliest gospel summary, 1 Corinthians 15:4, 'according to the Scriptures.'

The warning of verses 31 and 32 has parallels in Mark 3:28 to 30, which supplies the note that Jesus spoke because they were saying, 'He has an unclean spirit,' and in the hard passages of Hebrews 6:4 to 6 and 10:26 to 29. Acts 7:51 shows Stephen charging his hearers with always resisting the Holy Spirit. The family scene finds its sequel in Mark 3:21, where His family thought He was out of His mind, in John 7:5, where His brothers did not believe, and in Acts 1:14, where they are found praying with the disciples.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew places this controversy at the point where Jesus' ministry splits the nation into those who follow and those who oppose, and he wants his readers to know on which side the leaders stand and why. The point is not merely that the Pharisees were wrong. It is that they were wrong in the most dangerous way, by looking at the clear work of God's Spirit and naming it demonic. Matthew's first readers, Jewish Christians who were themselves being called deceivers by the synagogue leaders, needed to hear that the charge had already been made against their Master and had been answered.

He also means the section to shape how his readers speak. Verses 33 to 37 are not a rule about politeness. They teach that words are a window on the heart, so that a person cannot treat a verdict spoken about Jesus as a mere opinion. And the reference to the sign of Jonah prepares the church to understand its own central message: that the only proof Jesus offers a hardened generation is the resurrection, and that those who will not accept it will not be moved by any other.

The final scene is meant to redraw the boundaries of belonging for a community under pressure. Some of the new Christians would have been cut off from their families because of Jesus. Matthew wants them to know that the household they have lost is replaced by one in which Jesus Himself calls them mother, brother and sister, the family of those who do the Father's will.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The section describes a particular crisis, a miracle met with a slanderous charge, but it prescribes three things for every reader. First, it establishes a standard for the evaluation of any spiritual work: by their fruit, as Jesus teaches in verses 33 to 35, a work is to be judged by its character and by whether it aligns with Christ, not by whether it is spectacular. Second, it instructs the believer to take care over speech, since Jesus says careless words will be reckoned at the judgment. That is a call to a heart renewed, not to a nervous policing of every phrase. Third, it makes obedience to the Father the mark of belonging.

What should not be carried straight over is the report of the Pharisees' accusation or the specific scene of verse 46. Jesus' words to His mother and brothers are not a general permission to neglect natural family; He elsewhere rebukes those who dodge duty to parents, Mark 7:10 to 13, and from the cross He arranged for His mother's care, John 19:26 to 27. The exorcism and the strong man describe what the kingdom did in His ministry, and the church shares in it by the gospel, but believers are not told here to expect the same pattern of deliverance in every case. Finally, the unforgivable sin is described as a state of hardened rejection; it is not a command, and it should not be turned into a trap for the tender conscience.

debates.question: What is the blasphemy against the Spirit that will not be forgiven?

views.label: The hardened, deliberate attribution of the Spirit's work to Satan
views.case: In context it is exactly what the Pharisees do: seeing God's evident work through the Spirit and knowingly calling it demonic, a settled defiance that closes the heart to the only source of repentance.

views.label: A persistent, final rejection rather than one utterance
views.case: The unforgivable sin is not an isolated word but a fixed, ongoing refusal of the Spirit's testimony to Christ; those anxious that they have committed it show, by their very concern, a heart still tender.

debates.bearing: Both offer comfort to the troubled and warning to the hardened: the sin is a resolute, ongoing rejection of the Spirit's witness, not a slip of the tongue, and the willing sinner who turns to Christ is never turned away.

debates.question: How is the sign of Jonah fulfilled, and how is the three days reckoned?

views.label: The resurrection after burial
views.case: The sign is Jesus' death, burial, and rising; as Jonah emerged from the fish, so Jesus rises from the tomb, the decisive vindication offered to an unbelieving generation.

views.label: Three days and nights by inclusive reckoning
views.case: Jewish counting treated any part of a day as a day, so Friday to Sunday spans three days; the phrase heart of the earth need not require three full 24-hour periods.

debates.bearing: Both affirm that the one sign Jesus gives is His resurrection, the ground of Christian faith, foreshadowed by Jonah and proving Him greater than every prophet and king.

debates.question: Who are 'your sons' who drive out demons, verse 27?

views.label: Jewish exorcists of the Pharisees' own circle
views.case: The natural sense is that some Jewish practitioners, known to the Pharisees, were casting out spirits. Jesus presses a consistency argument: if the Pharisees do not call their work satanic, they have no ground to treat His differently, and so their own colleagues become their judges.

views.label: The disciples of Jesus, who were Jews of the same nation
views.case: Others note that the Twelve had been sent out to drive out demons in Matthew 10:1 and 10:8, and were also sons of Israel. On this reading the charge falls on those who cast out spirits in His name as well.

debates.bearing: Either way the force is the same. The charge of verse 24 condemns more than it intends, since it would also condemn every exorcist the Pharisees approved. It also clarifies that the real difference is not the act but the source, the Spirit of God, and the arrival of the kingdom that verse 28 announces.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb in the verse 28 clause is easy to miss. Jesus says the kingdom of God 'has come upon you,' using a Greek aorist form of phthano. The word means to arrive or to reach a point, and the aorist tense presents the arrival as an accomplished fact, not an approach. The kingdom is not about to come. In the act of this exorcism it has already reached them. The same verb in the same tense appears in Luke 11:20.

The verb for driving out, ekballo, is used five times in verses 24 to 28. It is the forceful word for throwing out or expelling, and it is the same verb used of the exorcisms throughout Matthew. Because it is repeated so often, the argument rolls forward like a series of hammer blows: if by Beelzebul, if by the Spirit, 'drive out.' The point is that the whole debate is about the source, not about whether it happened.

The saying of verse 30, 'He who does not gather with Me scatters,' is built on a contrast of two verbs, synago, to gather, and skorpizo, to scatter. It is the language of the shepherd and the harvest. It also sounds strange beside Mark 9:40, 'whoever is not against us is for us.' The two sayings are not rivals but answers to two different situations. Mark's is about a stranger who is already acting in Jesus' name; Matthew's is about the leaders who stand before Him and refuse to choose.

In verse 36 the 'careless word' is a rhema argon. Argos is made from the negative prefix and the word for work, so it means idle or unworking. Matthew uses the same word of the labourers standing idle in the marketplace in Matthew 20:3 and 20:6. A careless word is one that does no good work, the empty and unthinking remark. Jesus' point is that even this reveals the heart.

In verse 37 the two verbs, 'be acquitted' and 'be condemned,' are the language of the courtroom, the same family as 'righteous' in the Greek. Jesus uses the verb of justification for the final verdict on a person, with words as the evidence.

Verse 40 says 'belly of the great fish,' where the Greek word for the creature is ketos, the same word used in the Greek translation of Jonah 2:1. The phrase 'in the heart of the earth' echoes Jonah 2:3, 'the heart of the seas.' The 'three days and three nights' is a Semitic idiom; in Esther 4:16 the fast of 'three days, night or day' ends on 'the third day,' Esther 5:1, showing that part of a day could be counted as a whole.

Finally, in verses 41 and 42 the 'One greater' is in the Greek a neuter, something more than Jonah and something more than Solomon. The neuter points to the whole phenomenon of the kingdom and the person at its centre, and the same construction appears in verse 6, 'something greater than the temple.'

typology.type: Jonah in the great fish, Matthew 12:40
typology.fulfillment: Jonah was swallowed, and after three days and nights in the belly of the fish he was cast onto dry land to preach to Nineveh, Jonah 1:17 and 2:10. Jesus claims the story as a pattern for His own burial, and the New Testament understands His resurrection as raised on the third day, 1 Corinthians 15:4. The escalation is that Jonah's trial was a consequence of his own flight while Jesus' descent was a willing one for others, Philippians 2:8. The type also falls short because Jonah returned only to preach; Jesus rises as the Lord of the nations who sends His apostles to them, Matthew 28:19.

typology.type: The strong man bound and plundered, Matthew 12:29
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 49:24 to 25 asks whether plunder can be taken from the mighty and answers that the LORD Himself will retrieve it. Jesus presents His exorcisms as the first fruits of that rescue, the binding of the strong one so that his captives walk free. The picture is carried forward by Luke 10:18, where Satan falls like lightning, by Colossians 2:15, where the powers are disarmed at the cross, and by Revelation 20:1 to 3, where the dragon is bound for the thousand years. The type is not yet complete, since the enemy still prowls, 1 Peter 5:8, but the decisive binding has been made.

typology.type: Nineveh and the Queen of the South as witnesses
typology.fulfillment: Two Gentile figures are set as jurors against Israel's leaders. Nineveh believed God at one prophet's reluctant preaching, Jonah 3:5, and the queen travelled to test Solomon with hard questions, 1 Kings 10:1. They anticipate the Gentile pilgrims who will come to Christ from east and west, Matthew 8:11, and the nations that the Servant brings justice to, Matthew 12:18 and 12:21. The correspondence breaks down in that both were responding to a servant or a king of Israel, whereas the greater One here is the Lord of the nations Himself.

Isaiah 42:1 promised that God would put His Spirit on His chosen Servant, and Matthew has just quoted it. The Pharisees' blasphemy is thus a charge against the very anointing the prophet foretold. At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends, Matthew 3:16, and in the synagogue at Nazareth Luke has Jesus apply Isaiah 61:1 to Himself. The Servant's gentleness, the bruised reed that He will not break, does not contradict the strong man's binding; the same Spirit does both. Only the Servant who bears sin, Isaiah 53:12, fully matches this portrait.

The empty, swept and orderly house is a figure of Israel's reform without repentance. Isaiah 5:4 has the vineyard owner asking what more could have been done, and Jeremiah 3:20 portrays Israel as a faithless wife. A clean house with no occupant invites worse residents. The correspondence is fulfilled in the generation that heard Jesus: the nation tidied itself while declining the Lord who would fill it. The picture is a warning, not a prediction for every reformed person, and the gospel's answer is not a better-swept house but a house indwelt by the Spirit, Romans 8:9.

study.christ:
Jesus appears in this section as the Servant on whom the Spirit rests, and Matthew intends the reader to hear Isaiah 42 echoing through the whole controversy. When Jesus says that He drives out demons by the Spirit of God, He is not describing a borrowed power but the very anointing that the prophet promised, and the exorcism is the first sign that the age of the kingdom has begun. The same Gospel records the voice at His baptism and the descent of the Spirit, Matthew 3:16 to 17, so that the Pharisees' charge is aimed at a person whom the Father has publicly claimed.

He is also the stronger one of John the Baptist's announcement, Matthew 3:11. The picture of the strong man bound and plundered is the New Testament's way of describing what the cross and resurrection do. Luke has Satan falling like lightning, Luke 10:18, and John says that the Son of God appeared 'to destroy the works of the devil,' 1 John 3:8. Colossians 2:15 describes the stripping of the powers at the cross. In Jesus' hands even the ones He frees are a trophy of the victory, and the healing of the blind and mute man is the preview.

The statement that something greater than Jonah and something greater than Solomon is here is a claim of unmatched rank. Jonah was the reluctant prophet who preached judgment and mercy to a pagan city; Solomon was the king whose wisdom drew the world's rulers. Jesus is both prophet and wise king in one, and also the temple's Lord, verse 6. He will be rejected by the people He came for, and yet His rejection is the means by which the Gentiles come, a pattern that the sign of Jonah itself carries: the prophet is thrown into the deep, and the nations repent.

The sign is His own death and rising. Jesus will not offer more than that, and the New Testament follows His lead. The apostles do not preach a spectacular career but the empty tomb, and Paul stakes everything on it in 1 Corinthians 15:14. Acts 17:31 says God gave proof to everyone by raising Him from the dead. For those who see that sign and still refuse, no other will persuade.

The close of the chapter shows the Son's relationship to the Father in a new light. His claim on those who do the Father's will is not an alternative to His love for His own family; He is establishing that a family is formed around obedience to the Father, and He is the elder brother of that family. Hebrews 2:11 says He is not ashamed to call them brothers, and Romans 8:29 describes Him as the firstborn among many brothers. After the resurrection He uses the very word for His disciples, Matthew 28:10. A caution is needed: the empty house is not a coded image of the Spirit-less church, and the strong man is not an allegory for every detail of the cross. The links rest on the text's own claims.
study.god:
The section shows God as a King who has come in power. The kingdom of God, verse 28, is not a distant ideal but a present rule that is breaking into a captive world, and the Spirit is its agent. The doctrine of God that comes through is not a deity who is neutral in the contest between good and evil; He is the one who contends, who invades the strong man's house and who frees the captives. The Old Testament's promise that the LORD Himself will retrieve the plunder, Isaiah 49:25, is being kept in the ministry of the Son.

The three persons are at work together. The Spirit of God empowers the Son, the Son acts for the Father's kingdom, and the passage treats an offence against the Spirit as a distinct and weightier matter than an offence against the Son of Man, verse 32. That is why the passage has long been used in the church's reflection on the Trinity. The Spirit is not a force but the one who testifies to Christ and whose witness may be insulted, as Hebrews 10:29 says of 'the Spirit of grace.'

God is a judge for whom words matter. Because He searches the heart, Jeremiah 17:10, He knows what lies behind the speech, and verse 37 teaches that the final verdict will take account of what a person has said. This is not a God who is petty about slips of the tongue; it is one who treats the mouth as the overflow of the heart. The comfort goes with the seriousness: the same God has pledged forgiveness for 'every sin and blasphemy' that is brought to Him, verse 31, and has appointed a day when all will be set right.

God is also patient and persistent in mercy. Nineveh repented at the preaching of one reluctant prophet and God relented, Jonah 3:10, which shows that He is ready to forgive even the cruellest city. The judgment of the generation that heard Jesus is therefore not a failure of His mercy but the measure of its refusal.

He is a God who forms a family. The scene of verses 46 to 50 shows the Father calling out a household in which the Son is the elder brother. Obedience here is not a way of earning belonging but the evidence of it, as in Matthew 7:21. For worship, this means that the proper response to the wonder of the kingdom is neither the sceptic's demand for more proof nor the empty tidiness of the swept house, but a heart that is filled, a mouth that confesses, Romans 10:9 to 10, and a life that does the Father's will.

crossReferences.note: Matthew has just quoted this verse in 12:18, where God puts His Spirit on His chosen Servant. The Pharisees' charge in verse 24 is therefore a denial of the very anointing the prophet foretold, which is why Jesus reacts so severely when His Spirit-empowered work is called demonic.

The prophet asks whether plunder can be taken from the mighty and answers that the LORD will do it. Jesus' picture of tying up the strong man and plundering his house is a deliberate application: what God promised for Israel's captives is now being done by the Spirit's power in the exorcisms.

Pharaoh's own magicians recognised the finger of God in the plague of gnats, yet Pharaoh hardened his heart. Luke's parallel says Jesus drives out demons 'by the finger of God,' so the Pharisees are set beside Pharaoh: able to see the hand of God and still refusing.

Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish. Jesus takes this as the only sign He will give, a pointer to His burial and resurrection, and Jonah 2:3 supplies the phrase 'the heart of the seas' echoed in 'the heart of the earth.'

The Ninevites believed God, fasted and turned from their evil ways, and God relented. Jesus sets this repentance against the refusal of those who have seen far more than Jonah offered, so that pagans become the witnesses for the prosecution.

The queen of Sheba came with hard questions and left praising the LORD for His love for Israel. Jesus holds her up as an example of a seeker who travelled far for wisdom, over against leaders who had the greater wisdom standing in their midst and would not listen.

Mark explains why Jesus spoke: 'because they were saying, He has an unclean spirit.' This confirms that the unforgivable sin is tied to the specific act of attributing the Spirit's work to evil and shows the context in which the warning must be read.

The writer describes people who have tasted the heavenly gift and the Holy Spirit and then fall away, so that restoration to repentance becomes impossible. It sheds light on the same hardening, though the writer is describing a settled apostasy, not a lapse.

The Sermon on the Mount teaches that a tree is known by its fruit and that only he who does the will of the Father enters the kingdom. Jesus uses the same logic here for the Pharisees' words, and the closing family scene returns to the same phrase about doing the Father's will.

In Luke's version Jesus says He drives out demons 'by the finger of God,' where Matthew has 'the Spirit of God.' The two phrases interpret each other and link the exorcisms to the finger of God in Exodus 8:19, the mark of the divine hand.

Paul's earliest summary of the gospel says Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures. It shows how quickly the church fixed on the resurrection as the sign, just as Jesus had said in the Jonah saying.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning of Genesis the Bible has told of a contest between the offspring of the woman and the serpent, Genesis 3:15, and of a people held captive by a power they could not break. The exodus was a rescue from an oppressor, the prophets asked whether plunder could be taken from the mighty, Isaiah 49:24, and the whole story waits for the Servant on whom God's Spirit would rest. This section is where that long waiting reaches a decisive point. The first blow against the strong man is struck in the healing of the blind and mute man, and the kingdom of God, so long promised, is declared to have arrived.

It also shows how the old pattern of resistance repeats. Pharaoh's heart was hardened even in the presence of the finger of God, Exodus 8:19; Israel in the wilderness saw the works and still tested God; and the leaders of Jesus' day see the Spirit's work and call it demonic. The story of the whole Bible includes the sobering fact that proximity to God's work does not guarantee a response to it, and the warning about the swept house belongs with the prophets' laments that Israel reformed without returning.

What the section sets up is the rest of the Gospel. Matthew 13 will turn to parables, spoken to crowds who have heard and not understood, and the sign of Jonah will find its answer at the tomb, where the stone is rolled away and the guard story begins, Matthew 28:11 to 15. The nations that Jonah's Nineveh and Solomon's Sheba foreshadowed are gathered by the commission of Matthew 28:19. The new family of verses 46 to 50 becomes the church, the household of God, Ephesians 2:19, in which Jews and Gentiles are brothers and sisters of Christ, Hebrews 2:11.

The story ends in a world where the strong man is not merely bound but removed. Revelation 20:1 to 3 pictures the dragon bound and the Abyss sealed, and Revelation 20:10 pictures his final end. The one who spoke of the heart's overflow will give the final verdict in the light of the whole truth, and those whose words and lives showed a heart for the Father will find that the family they were given is the one that never ends, Revelation 21:7.

quiz.q: How did Jesus answer the charge that He cast out demons by Beelzebul?

options.text: A kingdom divided against itself cannot stand; He acts by the Spirit of God, having bound the strong man.
options.note: Verses 25-29 expose the absurdity and reveal the true source of His power.

options.text: He admitted the source of His power was uncertain.
options.note: He was clear it was the Spirit of God, not uncertain, and He exposed their charge as absurd.

options.text: He refused to respond to the accusation.
options.note: He answered at length, showing the charge was self-defeating.

options.text: He agreed that some of His power came from Satan.
options.note: He decisively denied it, attributing His work to the Spirit of God.

quiz.q: What is the blasphemy against the Spirit that will not be forgiven?

options.text: The hardened, deliberate rejection that calls the Spirit's evident work the devil's, as the Pharisees did.
options.note: Verses 31-32 warn of this settled defiance against the Spirit's witness.

options.text: Any single angry word spoken against God in a weak moment.
options.note: It is a settled, defiant rejection, not an isolated word; this understates the hardness involved.

options.text: Speaking a word against the Son of Man.
options.note: Jesus says that can be forgiven; the unforgivable sin is against the Spirit's clear testimony.

options.text: Failing to perform enough religious duties.
options.note: It concerns hardened rejection of the Spirit, not a shortage of religious works.

quiz.q: What did Jesus teach about our words?

options.text: Words flow from the heart and reveal it, so we are acquitted or condemned by them.
options.note: Verses 34-37 tie speech to the overflow of the heart and to judgment.

options.text: Words are unimportant as long as actions are good.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus says even careless words will be accounted for because they reveal the heart.

options.text: Only public speeches, not private words, matter to God.
options.note: He warns of every careless word, not only public speech.

options.text: God pays no attention to what people say.
options.note: Jesus says we give account for our words on the day of judgment.

quiz.q: What sign did Jesus promise the sign-seeking generation?

options.text: Only the sign of Jonah, His three days in the earth and His resurrection.
options.note: Verses 39-40 give the sign of Jonah as pointing to His burial and rising.

options.text: A dramatic display of fire from heaven.
options.note: He refused spectacular signs, giving only the sign of Jonah, His resurrection.

options.text: No sign of any kind whatsoever.
options.note: He did promise one sign, the sign of Jonah, though He refused their demand for a spectacle.

options.text: The immediate overthrow of Rome.
options.note: The sign was His resurrection, not political conquest.

quiz.q: Who did Jesus say are His true family?

options.text: Whoever does the will of His Father in heaven is His brother, sister, and mother.
options.note: Verses 48-50 redefine family around doing the Father's will.

options.text: Only His biological mother and brothers.
options.note: He pointed beyond biological ties to those who do the Father's will.

options.text: Only the twelve apostles, and no others.
options.note: He included all who do the Father's will, not only the twelve.

options.text: Anyone who admires Him from a distance.
options.note: True kinship is doing the Father's will, not mere admiration.

questions: The Pharisees saw undeniable good and called it evil to protect themselves. Where are you tempted to explain away God's work because acknowledging it would cost you something?
Jesus said words flow from the heart. What do your habitual words reveal about the state of your heart, and where do you need God to change it?
The only sign Jesus gave was His resurrection. How does the historical reality of the empty tomb anchor your faith when you are tempted to want other proofs?
The empty, swept house ended worse than before because it was left vacant. How are you not just removing sin but filling your life with Christ and His Spirit?
Jesus welcomes into His family all who do the Father's will. What does it mean to you that obedience to God makes you a brother or sister of Jesus Himself?

translationNotes.note: Beelzebul is a name for the prince of demons, that is, Satan; the Pharisees credit the Spirit's work to him, the charge Jesus warns against.
Three days and three nights follows Jewish inclusive reckoning, in which any part of a day counts as a day; the sign points to Jesus' burial and resurrection.
Some early manuscripts do not include verse 47, as the BSB footnote notes; the sense continues unbroken into Jesus' reply about His true family.
